title: App Router vs Pages Router
summary: Next.js has two routing systems: the older **Pages Router** (`pages/`) built on client components with `getServerSideProps`/`getStaticProps` data functions, and the newer **App Router** (`app/`) built on **React Server Components**, with **nested layouts** and file conventions for **loading**, **error**, and data fetched directly in **async components**. New apps should use the App Router; the Pages Router remains for legacy code.

subtopics.title: Two directories, two systems
subtopics.explanation: The Pages Router lives in pages/ and the App Router lives in app/. They can even coexist in one project. The App Router (default and recommended since Next 13/14) is built on React Server Components and modern data fetching; the Pages Router is the original, client-component-based system that still works for legacy apps.
subtopics.example:
pages/index.tsx   -> Pages Router route /
app/page.tsx      -> App Router route /

subtopics.title: Server Components by default (App Router)
subtopics.explanation: In the App Router every component is a React Server Component unless you add 'use client'. Server Components run only on the server, never ship their JS to the browser, and can fetch data directly. The Pages Router has no Server Components — its components are client components that hydrate fully, even when only displaying static data.

subtopics.title: Nested layouts
subtopics.explanation: The App Router introduces layout.tsx files that wrap a route segment and all its children, and crucially persist across navigation without re-rendering. Layouts nest, so you can compose a root layout, a section layout, and a page. The Pages Router has only a single global _app.tsx and manual layout patterns, with no built-in nested, persistent layouts.

subtopics.title: loading and error conventions
subtopics.explanation: The App Router adds special files: loading.tsx automatically shows a fallback (via React Suspense) while a segment loads, and error.tsx (a Client Component) catches errors in that segment and renders a fallback UI. The Pages Router has none of these conventions — you wire up loading and error states manually in each page.
subtopics.example:
// app/dashboard/loading.tsx — shown automatically while the page loads export default function Loading() { return

Loading…

; }

subtopics.title: Data fetching: getServerSideProps/getStaticProps vs async components
subtopics.explanation: The Pages Router fetches data with exported functions: getServerSideProps (per request, SSR), getStaticProps (build time, SSG), and getStaticPaths (dynamic static routes). The App Router replaces all of these: you simply make the Server Component async and await fetch, and the rendering mode (SSG/ISR/SSR) follows the fetch's caching options.
subtopics.example:
// Pages: export async function getServerSideProps() { return { props } }
// App:   const data = await fetch(url, { cache: 'no-store' }); // SSR

subtopics.title: When to use each
subtopics.explanation: Use the App Router for all new projects: it has Server Components, nested layouts, streaming, and is where Next.js development is focused. Stay on (or keep) the Pages Router only for existing apps that are not yet migrated, or when a dependency hasn't caught up to Server Components. They can run side by side during a transition.
subtopics.example: // New app: prefer app/.  Existing app/: migrate incrementally.

subtopics.title: Migrating from Pages to App
subtopics.explanation: Migration is incremental: app/ and pages/ coexist, so you move routes one at a time. Convert getStaticProps to a cached async fetch, getServerSideProps to a no-store fetch or force-dynamic, _app/_document to root layout.tsx, and add 'use client' to components that use hooks, browser APIs, or event handlers. Move data fetching down into the components that need it.

foundations.overview: Next.js ships two routing paradigms. The Pages Router (pages/) is the original system: client components plus special data functions (getServerSideProps, getStaticProps). The App Router (app/) is the modern default: React Server Components, nested persistent layouts, file conventions for loading/error/not-found, and data fetched directly inside async server components. Choosing and understanding both is core to working in any Next.js codebase.
foundations.formalDefinition: The Pages Router maps files in pages/ to routes, treating each page as a client component and using exported lifecycle functions for server/static data. The App Router maps folders in app/ to route segments, defaulting components to Server Components, composing nested layouts, and deriving rendering mode from fetch caching rather than dedicated data functions.
foundations.whyItMatters: Most production Next.js code today is being written in or migrated to the App Router, but huge amounts of Pages Router code still exist. Engineers must read both, know the data-fetching differences, and migrate safely — making this a high-frequency interview and on-the-job topic.
foundations.mentalModel: Pages Router = 'pages are client components; ask for server/static data via special functions.' App Router = 'components are server-first; fetch data right where you render, wrap routes in nested layouts, and let conventions handle loading/error.'
foundations.browserPerspective: With the App Router, Server Components produce HTML without shipping their JS, so the browser downloads less and hydrates only Client Components. With the Pages Router every page hydrates as a full client component, so more JavaScript is shipped even for static content.
foundations.realWorldUsage: New SaaS, commerce, and content apps are built on the App Router for its layouts and server components; legacy enterprise apps often remain on the Pages Router and migrate route-by-route as time allows.
foundations.businessImpact: The App Router's smaller client bundles and built-in streaming/layout features improve performance and developer velocity; well-planned migration avoids costly rewrites by allowing incremental adoption.
foundations.engineeringImpact: The App Router changes the mental model from data-fetching functions to async server components and the server/client boundary. Teams must learn where code runs ('use client') and rethink layouts and loading states around conventions.
foundations.performanceImpact: App Router Server Components cut client JS and enable streaming and partial rendering, generally improving TTFB and hydration cost versus the Pages Router, where every page hydrates fully on the client.
commonUseCases: New projects standardizing on the App Router for Server Components and layouts
Legacy apps maintaining the Pages Router while migrating incrementally
Shared layouts (nav, sidebars) that persist across navigation via App Router layouts
Per-segment loading and error UI using App Router conventions

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must rewrite the whole app to adopt the App Router.
commonMisconceptions.reality: app/ and pages/ coexist in the same project, so you migrate one route at a time.

commonMisconceptions.myth: App Router components are client components like the Pages Router.
commonMisconceptions.reality: App Router components are Server Components by default; you opt into client behavior explicitly with 'use client'.

steps.detail: Pages: getServerSideProps / getStaticProps / getStaticPaths. App: await fetch inside async Server Components, mode set by caching.

steps.name: Choosing
steps.detail: New apps -> App Router. Legacy code -> Pages Router, migrated incrementally since both can coexist.

debuggingLab.title: useState crashes in an App Router Server Component
debuggingLab.symptom: After moving a page to app/, it throws an error like 'useState is not a function' / 'You're importing a component that needs useState. It only works in a Client Component'.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: In the App Router components are Server Components unless you add 'use client'. Server Components run only on the server and cannot use hooks (useState/useEffect), event handlers, or browser APIs. Using useState without 'use client' is therefore an error.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that App Router components default to the server, unlike Pages Router pages.
Putting interactivity in a Server Component instead of extracting it into a 'use client' component.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Mark the interactive component as a Client Component by adding 'use client' at the top of the file.

theory.question: What are the main differences between the App Router and the Pages Router?
theory.directAnswer: The Pages Router (pages/) treats each page as a client component and fetches data via exported functions (getServerSideProps, getStaticProps, getStaticPaths). The App Router (app/) makes components React Server Components by default, fetches data directly inside async components (with caching deciding SSG/ISR/SSR), and adds nested persistent layouts plus file conventions for loading, error, and not-found. The App Router is the modern default; both can coexist for incremental migration.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two routing systems differing in component model (server-first vs client), data fetching, layouts, and built-in conventions.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The App Router was introduced to bring React Server Components, streaming, and nested layouts to Next.js while keeping the Pages Router for backward compatibility.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: app/ uses folders as segments with page/layout/loading/error files and server-first rendering; pages/ uses files as routes with client components and data functions.

theory.whyImportant: It is the defining structural decision in modern Next.js and a top interview topic; you must understand both to read and migrate real codebases.
theory.realWorldExample: A team migrating a dashboard moves /settings to app/settings/page.tsx, replaces getServerSideProps with a no-store fetch, and adds a shared app/settings/layout.tsx for the persistent sidebar.

nestedTopics.title: Server vs client default
nestedTopics.explanation: App Router defaults to Server Components; Pages Router pages are client components.

nestedTopics.title: Layouts
nestedTopics.explanation: App Router nests persistent layout.tsx files; Pages Router has a single _app.tsx.

nestedTopics.title: Conventions
nestedTopics.explanation: loading.tsx, error.tsx, not-found.tsx are App-Router-only file conventions.

followUps.question: Can both routers exist in one project?
followUps.answer: Yes — app/ and pages/ coexist, which is exactly how incremental migration works.

followUps.question: Which should new projects use?
followUps.answer: The App Router; it is the default and where new Next.js features land.

theory.question: How does data fetching differ between the two routers?
theory.directAnswer: In the Pages Router you export data functions: getStaticProps runs at build time (SSG), getServerSideProps runs per request (SSR), and getStaticPaths defines dynamic static routes; the data is passed as props. In the App Router there are no such functions — you make the Server Component async and await fetch directly, and the rendering mode is derived from the fetch's caching (default = SSG, next.revalidate = ISR, no-store/force-dynamic = SSR).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two different mechanisms for getting server/static data into a page.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The App Router unifies fetching into the component model so data lives where it's used, instead of in separate exported functions.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Caching options on fetch (or route segment config) replace the dedicated Pages Router data functions.

theory.whyImportant: Data fetching is the part developers touch most when migrating; interviewers probe whether you can map the old functions to the new model.
theory.realWorldExample: getStaticProps with revalidate: 60 becomes await fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 60 } }) inside the async Server Component.

nestedTopics.title: Caching = rendering mode
nestedTopics.explanation: In the App Router the fetch's cache option determines SSG vs ISR vs SSR.

nestedTopics.title: Colocated fetching
nestedTopics.explanation: Each component fetches its own data rather than a single page-level function.

followUps.question: What replaces getStaticPaths?
followUps.answer: generateStaticParams in the App Router pre-generates dynamic segment values at build time.

scenario.question: You inherit a large Pages Router app and want to adopt the App Router. How do you migrate without a risky big-bang rewrite?
scenario.directAnswer: Migrate incrementally, because app/ and pages/ can coexist. I'd start by creating app/layout.tsx (replacing _app/_document), then move low-risk routes first, converting getStaticProps to cached fetches and getServerSideProps to no-store/force-dynamic. I'd add 'use client' only to components that need hooks, events, or browser APIs, push data fetching down into the components that need it, and adopt loading/error conventions per segment. Each route ships and is verified independently.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A route-by-route migration leveraging coexisting routers.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Big-bang rewrites are risky; Next.js explicitly supports gradual adoption.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Move one route to app/, translate its data functions and layout, mark client components, then delete the old pages/ route.

scenario.whyImportant: Migration strategy is a realistic senior-level question that tests pragmatism, not just API knowledge.

nestedTopics.title: Coexistence
nestedTopics.explanation: Both routers run together so you migrate gradually.

nestedTopics.title: Client boundary
nestedTopics.explanation: Add 'use client' only where interactivity actually lives.

followUps.question: How do you decide which routes to migrate first?
followUps.answer: Start with simple, low-traffic, or self-contained routes to build confidence before tackling complex, high-traffic ones.

coding.question: Convert a Pages Router page using getServerSideProps into an App Router page.
coding.thoughtProcess: The Pages Router fetches per request via getServerSideProps and passes props. In the App Router I make the component async, fetch directly, and use cache: 'no-store' to keep it per-request (SSR). No exported data function is needed.
coding.lineByLine: The Pages version exports getServerSideProps to fetch per request and passes products as props. The App version drops that function: the page becomes async, fetches directly with cache: 'no-store' to remain SSR, and renders the result — data fetching now lives inside the component.
coding.timeComplexity: N/A — framework conversion, not an algorithm.

alternativeApproaches.title: Route segment config for SSR
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Instead of per-fetch no-store, force dynamic rendering for the whole route.

followUps.question: How would you make this ISR instead of SSR?
followUps.answer: Replace cache: 'no-store' with { next: { revalidate: 60 } } so the page is static but regenerates every 60 seconds.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Standardize new code on the App Router: a root app/layout.tsx, nested layouts per section, Server Components for data and Client Components for interactivity, and loading/error conventions per segment. During migration, keep pages/ alongside app/ and move routes incrementally rather than maintaining two divergent patterns long-term.
productionDeepDive.performance: The App Router reduces client JS because Server Components don't hydrate, and it supports streaming so users see content sooner. Keep Client Components small and push data fetching to the server. The Pages Router hydrates every page fully, so it ships more JS for equivalent static content.
productionDeepDive.security: App Router Server Components and route handlers run only on the server — keep secrets and data access there and never leak them into 'use client' components. The same discipline applies in the Pages Router's getServerSideProps/API routes.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Both routers serve static/ISR pages from the CDN cheaply and SSR via serverless/server compute. The App Router's finer-grained server/client split and streaming can reduce client cost; plan migrations so high-traffic routes are validated carefully.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Pick one router as the standard to avoid two mental models in one codebase. The App Router's conventions (layout/loading/error) make structure explicit; document any route that opts into dynamic rendering and why.
productionDeepDive.observability: Build output marks each route static or dynamic regardless of router. Monitor hydration cost, TTFB, and error rates; during migration, watch for regressions per migrated route before removing the old pages/ version.

caseStudies.problem: A Pages Router app needs Server Components, nested layouts, and smaller bundles without a risky rewrite.
caseStudies.solution: Incremental migration: coexist app/ and pages/, convert data functions to fetch caching, extract client components, and move routes one at a time.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Temporarily maintaining two routers and a learning curve for the server/client boundary, in exchange for performance and modern features.
caseStudies.lessons: Migrate gradually, validate per route, and standardize on the App Router as the long-term target.

keyTakeaways: Next.js has two routers: the legacy Pages Router (pages/, client components, getServerSideProps/getStaticProps) and the modern App Router (app/, Server Components by default).
App Router data fetching happens inside async Server Components, with the fetch's caching deciding SSG/ISR/SSR — replacing the Pages Router's data functions.
The App Router adds nested persistent layouts and file conventions (loading.tsx, error.tsx, not-found.tsx) that the Pages Router lacks.
App Router components default to the server; add 'use client' only where you need hooks, events, or browser APIs.
Use the App Router for new apps; migrate legacy Pages Router code incrementally since both routers can coexist in one project.
